title: Land Grabbers and the Gathered Flock
overview: Micah condemns powerful people who seize their neighbors' land and homes, warns they will lose their own, mocks their taste for comforting prophets, and ends with a picture of God gathering and leading a remnant.

parts.label: Schemes made at night (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Wealthy, powerful people lie awake planning how to take other families' fields and houses, then do it at dawn simply because no one can stop them. In Israel, family land was an inheritance meant to stay in the family for generations, so taking it robbed children and grandchildren too.

parts.label: A punishment that matches (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: The wording mirrors the crime: they plan evil, so the LORD plans disaster, and those who took land will see their own land divided among strangers. When land is shared out by lot, an old way of assigning family plots, they will have no one to claim a share for them.

parts.label: Stop preaching at us (vv. 6-7)
parts.note: Micah's listeners tell him to stop prophesying such gloomy things, insisting disgrace will never reach them. The LORD answers that his words are good for people who live rightly, so the threats say more about the hearers than about him; the Hebrew here is difficult, and translations differ on who is speaking.

parts.label: The victims named (vv. 8-10)
parts.note: The people have turned on their own like an enemy army, stripping cloaks off peaceful travelers and evicting women and children from their homes. The command to get up and leave turns their actions back on them: those who drove others out will be driven from a land they have spoiled.

parts.label: The prophet they want (v. 11)
parts.note: With biting sarcasm, Micah says the ideal prophet for this crowd would be a liar promising plenty of wine and beer. They want comfort, not truth.

parts.label: God gathers his flock (vv. 12-13)
parts.note: Suddenly the tone shifts to the LORD gathering what is left of his people like sheep in a pen, while a leader breaks through the gate ahead of them and their king leads them out. Scholars debate whether this is a real promise of hope, the false prophets' words being quoted, or even a picture of being herded into exile, and many Christians have read the figure who breaks through as pointing to Jesus.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the gathering in verses 12 and 13 refers to Israel's return from exile, to the church, or to a future restoration of the Jewish people.
think: When someone has the power to take something and no law will stop them, what, if anything, should still hold them back?
